transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Recording: yes
Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Evan Zhao (Redwood SRE), Olivia Grant (Redwood PM), Dana Murphy (Orion Eng Mgr), Ravi Shah (Orion ML Infra), Lena Gomez (Orion CTO), Alex (Orion intern)

Summary:
A technical deep dive focused on intermittent OOMs, CUDA driver errors, and timeout/retry behaviors observed by Orion Analytics on Redwood Dedicated nodes. Covered runtime batching/KV cache interactions, quantization fallbacks, pinned memory vs pageable memory, and recommended retry semantics. Agreed next steps to collect kernel traces and reproduce under dedicated capacity; plan to test with quantized + unquantized variants.

Topics: runtime performance, latency/throughput, KV cache, batching, quantization, VPC/on-prem constraints, OOMs, timeouts, CUDA errors, retry semantics

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Marcus: ok hi everyone thanks for joining, let's do quick intros, um, and then dive into the repro that you sent over yesterday.
[00:07] Dana: hi this is Dana, engineering manager on Orion, thanks for taking the time.
[00:10] Ravi: ravi here, ml infra. we saw both OOMs and occasional cuda driver resets when running our 8k context workload.
[00:16] Lena: lena, cto. hoping we can get to a stable baseline for production.
[00:20] Priya: Priya from Redwood, i'll walk through runtime logs and some hypotheses about fragmentation and kv cache pressure.
[00:25] Evan: Evan, SRE, i'll talk about retry semantics and how we instrument timeouts in the serving runtime.
[00:30] Alex: alex here, quick note: i posted the failing request ids in the slack thread.

[00:36] Speaker 1: ok jumping into the repro notes — so this was a 4-shard A100 setup, model is a 60B open model, using 4-bit quantization via our custom q4 recipe. batch size varied 1-8 across tests, sequence length up to 8k tokens. failures at high token counts.
[01:02] Ravi: yeah, failures cluster when a long prefix hits the kv cache warmup and then we start concurrent generation requests; we see cudaErrorOutOfMemory or sometimes the driver resets.
[01:14] Priya: two quick clarifying q's: is the kv cache enabled across requests or do you pin a prefix to the cache? do you use Redis or local fs for cache?
[01:22] Ravi: it's local in-memory kv cache on the instance. not Redis. prefix caching is enabled automatically by our client.
[01:27] Priya: got it. ok that helps.

[01:30] Marcus: can you paste the exact error snippet you saw? sometimes the logs show cuda out of memory at kernel launch and sometimes it's a driver timeout, those have different causes.
[01:39] Ravi: sure, pasted in slack but the short one is: "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 2.1 GiB (GPU 0; 40.00 GiB total capacity; 35.3 GiB already allocated; 0 bytes free; if reserved, try emptying cache)" and another: "Erl: [CUDA Driver] GPU watchdog timeout, GPU reset".
[01:56] Priya: ok classic. couple things to unpack: fragmentation vs real peak; quantize paths sometimes allocate intermediate float buffers (especially during kv cache merging or resharding) so even q4 can spike memory. second, pinned host pinned memory allocations can fail if pageable pool is small and we end up staging copies.
[02:14] Dana: can you explain the kv cache behavior — when a request hits and there's a cache miss we materialize a prefix, does that temporarily double memory?
[02:22] Priya: yeah so when we materialize a prefix for generation we often keep the original tensors plus the compact kv representation until we garbage collect; if multiple requests race to warm the cache we can have multiple copies of similar kv pages. batching increases the concurrency window so you can get N copies.
[02:36] Marcus: also, if you have cross-request batching the runtime merges KV shards for fused attention kernels which may create transient buffers proportional to sum of sequence lengths for the batch. that's a common OOM vector at high seq len.
[02:49] Ravi: that matches. failures spike when batch size is 4-8 and seq length ~6k. single requests at 1 seem fine most of time.

[02:58] Evan: regarding timeouts, we set a soft server-side token generation timeout default at 60s and a hard cutoff at 120s for hosted customers; Dedicated configs can change that. If kernels hang or driver resets happen, the request thread can be stuck waiting and the client may retry which exacerbates pressure. we recommend idempotency tokens on client side and exponential backoff with jitter.
[03:18] Lena: the client currently retries immediately twice. that sounds bad.
[03:22] Marcus: immediate retries are a killer here — they multiply memory and kernel concurrency. we should recommend linear/exponential backoff and check for explicit error types before retrying (e.g., don't retry driver-reset without escalation).
[03:33] Priya: one engineering mitigation is to prefer single-request passthrough for very long sequences, i.e., avoid batching those long requests with others in the same micro-batch. Redwood runtime has a per-request batching policy — we can set a sequence-length cutoff so requests longer than X are isolated.
[03:48] Ravi: can you set that per model? per route?
[03:51] Priya: yes per route and per model config. we can push a canary config to your dedicated pool.

[03:56] Speaker 1: there's also quantization fallback: when we detect kernel mismatch or instability we sometimes decompress to fp16 for stability — that can spike memory. do you have logs showing quantization warnings?
[04:06] Ravi: we do see a few "quantization profile mismatch, falling back to fp16" warnings in the same timeframe.
[04:12] Priya: that's critical. fallback increases memory footprint and reduces capacity; if fallback happens mid-batch it will blow past expectations. we should try to eliminate fallback by pinning a consistent quantization config across the pipeline, or pre-warm and validate kernels in a smoke test.
[04:27] Marcus: to add, kernel selection mismatch can be due to small compiler flags, cudnn versions, or a mixed driver update across nodes. are all nodes on the same driver?
[04:36] Ravi: nodes are supposed to be consistent but we did one rolling driver update last week; i'm not 100% sure the dedicated pool was fully homogeneous.
[04:42] Evan: that can absolutely cause nondeterministic kernel selector behavior and intermittent fallbacks; also be mindful of docker image layers that may have different CUDA toolkit minor versions.
[04:52] Dana: noted, we'll verify.

[04:55] Priya: actionable runbook items: 1) reproduce deterministically with a canary workload pinned to a single node; 2) capture nvprof/cupti traces during the failure; 3) enable our verbose kernel selection logs; 4) temporarily disable cross-request batching for long seqs.
[05:13] Marcus: also collect GPU memory fragmentation stats (nvidia-smi --memory-usage doesn't show fragmentation), use nvml APIs or our agent to look at reserved vs committed vs mapped.
[05:24] Ravi: ok we'll run NVML exports and upload to the shared drive.

[05:29] Alex: quick question — does the KV cache eviction policy ever cause spikes? like when eviction runs we copy pages?
[05:34] Priya: eviction itself shouldn't allocate big buffers, but if eviction triggers compaction we may allocate temporary buffers. our current compaction is conservative; we can change to streaming compaction to reduce spikes.
[05:45] Lena: what about pinned memory exhaustion — is that common?
[05:48] Priya: yes if you do a lot of host->device async copies and the host side uses pinned buffers, the OS pinned pool can saturate; that leads to failed CUDAHostAlloc and then we try fallback paths. on some kernel paths we also use pinned memory for zero-copy IO to reduce latency which trades off against stability under high concurrency.
[06:07] Marcus: another tip: consider cgroups and per-container GPU memory accounting; we can throttle per-container allocations so a runaway client can't exhaust the whole card.
[06:16] Evan: on retry semantics again — we instrument request metadata with a retry_count header and a partial_liveness flag so the runtime knows not to schedule retries blindly. i.e., if retry_count > 0 we prefer isolated scheduling to avoid re-amplification.
[06:31] Ravi: that's useful, how do we get that in our client?
[06:34] Marcus: we'll share the SDK snippet. we'll also recommend the idempotency-token header and a 500 vs 503 mapping guide. don't retry on 500 if it's a driver reset, escalate to support.
[06:45] Priya: there were a couple of interesting logs where the runtime timed out waiting for a kernel to complete (hang), we then killed the process and the gpu reset. those correlate with specific attention kernels at large sequence lengths — we've seen some kernels degrade >O(n^2) behavior in pathological inputs due to indexing edge cases.
[07:02] Ravi: oh interesting, any mitigation?
[07:04] Priya: patching kernels is medium-term; short-term we can isolate long sequences and force smaller micro-batches or use attention recomputation (trading latency for memory) which avoids the big transient buffers. another option is to use a different kernel path for long sequences (we have a streaming attention kernel that is more memory friendly).
[07:23] Lena: does that affect latency badly?
[07:25] Priya: streaming attention increases per-token compute slightly but reduces peak memory by 30-50% depending on config; so latency per token may increase ~10-20% but avoids OOMs. for interactive workloads that may be acceptable.
[07:39] Marcus: on the on-prem/VPC side, are there additional constraints? network-mounted cache or NFS can cause stalls and exacerbate timeouts.
[07:47] Ravi: we're using local instance store, not NFS, but our control-plane in VPC talks to an internal Redis for metadata. latency there is low but we'd like to avoid cross-AZ calls.
[07:58] Evan: for Dedicated we can pin control-plane traffic to same AZ and use eBPF tracing to ensure no network stalls. also enable per-request tracing to correlate kernel spikes with network events.
[08:10] Speaker 1: quick interjection: we saw a case where a bad client payload repeatedly requested forced attention window sizes and the model ended up taking extreme memory — client-side validation to cap seq length is important.
[08:21] Dana: we have client checks but there were some migration scripts that bypassed them. we'll audit.

[08:27] Priya: i want to call out quantization testing: your q4 pipeline is great for throughput but it's brittle if quantization profiles mismatch across library versions. do a deterministic quantization validation: run a small synthetic check that compares q4 outputs vs fp16 to ensure kernel parity before rolling.
[08:45] Ravi: is there a Redwood tool to do that?
[08:48] Priya: yes we have a quantization sanity harness — i'll drop the link after the call (see artifacts below). it runs micro-benchmarks and verifies no fallback warnings.

[08:55] Marcus: artifacts: we will share a doc with recommended runtime flags (--batching-policy, --seq-cutoff, --streaming-attention), a small SDK snippet for idempotency tokens and exponential backoff, and the quantization sanity harness link: https://redwood.internal/quant-harness (internal) and the repro template: https://redwood.internal/repro-templates/orion-oom-2025-03 (canary).
[09:18] Alex: thanks.

[09:22] Evan: one more operational note — enable our verbose gpu-agent which collects NVML counters per second (reserved, committed, mapped) and also reports host pinned memory usage. that extra telemetry made one customer find a host leak quickly.
[09:36] Ravi: okay we'll enable that on the dedicated pool. what's the overhead?
[09:40] Evan: minimal, <1% CPU and a few MB of host memory.

[09:45] Lena: any hard limits we should set at the runtime level?
[09:48] Priya: set a per-request GPU reservation cap (e.g., 32 GiB for this model on 40 GiB cards) and a per-route max concurrent requests. that prevents a single request from ballooning the whole device if fallback happens.
[10:00] Marcus: also configure a safe fallback strategy: prefer graceful degrade to streaming-attention over immediate decompress-to-fp16 fallback. reorder preference: streaming -> recompute -> fp16 fallback.
[10:11] Dana: good to have prioritization.

[10:15] Speaker 1: question from chat — what about CUDA kernel timeouts (TDR) on Windows-like hosts? we're linux though.
[10:21] Evan: on cloud linux we don't hit TDR same as windows but GPU watchdog can still trigger if kernel exceeds watchdog threshold. on the runtime we cap per-kernel time and break up long kernels where possible.
[10:33] Marcus: ok let's recap and make sure we have clear next steps.

- Priya will run the repro on a dedicated node, collect nvprof/cupti traces and verbose kernel selection logs, and upload by 2025-03-15.
